title: Simple 3D Imaging of Biogenic Silica Structures by Fluorescence Microscopy
author: Sebastien Colin
license_note: Confirmed via CrossRef DOI metadata: dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.vuze6x6
materials: Preparation of the dye. The staining strategy relies on the electrostatic binding of the polymer poly-L-lysine on silica surface in water at neutral pH. Hence, the poly-L-lysine (PLL) polymer is conjugated with fluorochromes molecules to allow its visualization by fluorescent microscopy. A wide variety of amine-reactive fluorescent dyes are commercially available for conjugation to proteins which allows a high flexibility regarding spectral properties of the fluorochrome moiety. The conjugation reaction on a poly-amine protein is then trivial and the different reagents are affordable. The preparation of the conjugate is described by Colin et al. (2017), doi:10.7554/eLife.26066. Briefly, in that case, the fluorescent dye moiety was an Alexa Fluor 546 NHS succinimidyl ester (AF546SE, Invitrogen A20002; Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). The PLL (Sigma-Aldrich P5899; Merck, Germany) display an average length of 2,340 lysine unit. The conjugation reaction was performed according to the AF546 provider’s protocol for protein conjugation. The ratio [R-NH2]/[AF546SE] was calculated to generate the statistical binding of one AF546 per 1500 lysine units. The stock solution of this conjugate was kept at −20°C.

steps.title: Prepare biogenic silica particles
steps.instruction: Clean the silica particles to remove organic materials and prepare a suspension in double-distilled or ultrapure water (dd-H2O).

substeps.instruction: For particles from living organisms, remove organic materials using acidic, oxidizing, detergent, or solvent treatments.
For mineral micro-fossils or sediments, perform a quick water washing step.
Ensure the final product is a suspension of clean particles in dd-H2O.

steps.title: Stain silica particles
steps.instruction: Label the silica particles using a PLL-A546 conjugate solution.

substeps.instruction: Resuspend a few milligrams of silica particles in 1 ml of dd-H2O in a 2 ml microcentrifuge tube (adapt volume/tube size lower for single isolated objects).
Allow particles to sediment and gently remove the supernatant (optionally use pipette tips capped by a 1 µm mesh piece to avoid loss).
Resuspend particles in 500 µl of staining mix (500 µl dd-H2O + 5 µl PLL-A546 conjugate solution); for single isolated micro-structures, use 25 µl of similar staining solution.
Incubate the tube for at least 1/2 hour at room temperature in the dark, flipping the tube occasionally to homogenize.
Allow particles to sediment, remove the staining solution, and rinse particles with 2 ml of dd-H2O.
Repeat the washing step at least twice, protecting particles from light to avoid photobleaching.

steps.title: Store labeled particles
steps.instruction: If not imaging immediately, store the labeled particles in dd-H2O at 4°C in the dark.

steps.title: Mount specimens for 3D imaging
steps.instruction: Select a mounting method based on the microscope and objective specifications.

substeps.instruction: For water immersion objectives: Load the suspension of particles into an observation container (e.g., petri dish or multi-well plate with a high-quality glass bottom close to coverslip #1.5H) and image directly in water.

For refractive index matching (glass): Load particles into the observation container, remove liquid, and oven dry at ~50°C for a few hours or overnight, then mount in immersion oil or other compatible mounting media.
For opaline refractive index (1.42 to 1.47): Use glycerin mounting with a glycerin immersion objective.
For light-sheet microscopy: Use hydrogel embedding (e.g., agarose, phytagel, polyacrylamide).

steps.title: Perform 3D imaging
steps.instruction: Use a fluorescence microscopy modality capable of 3D tomography by optical sectioning.

substeps.instruction: Use confocal laser scanning microscopy (single or multipoint) for standard 3D tomography.
Use multiphoton microscopy for deeper penetration into thick specimens.
Use multi-angle light-sheet microscopy for scattering specimens and isotropic reconstruction.
